ma_dogtown.blurb: Dogtown is pure bouldering: hard Cape Ann granite blocks, left behind by retreating ice, scattered through roughly 3,600 acres of tangled woods between Gloucester and Rockport. The terrain is rugged and rocky, many of the clusters lie off the trails, and the boulders are spread widely, so a session usually involves real walking between groups. Problems run from V0 up to about V8, with the bulk between V3 and V6. The larger clusters include Rifle Range Boulders, Wine Brook, Pool Hill Forest and Dory Road Boulders, while many smaller groups hold only a handful of problems each. The setting has an old, eerie feel.

wi_northern_highlands.blurb: The Northern Highlands is bouldering in Wisconsin's North Woods, where the remains of ancient mountain ranges show up as scattered boulders across a wide area. Nearly everything is a boulder problem, from the easiest grades to about V11, with most between V0 and V5. Rib Mountain, near Wausau, is the biggest zone: white quartzite with problems of many kinds, a place to wander with a pad and try things, and some lines tall enough that a rope is a sensible backup. Locals have bouldered there since the 1970s. Chute Pond County Park, Hagar Mountain and Dave's Falls County Park add further groups, so the region is spread out and rewards a few days of exploring.

bc_columbia_shushwap.blurb: Columbia-Shuswap spans several very different mountain scenes in the interior of British Columbia. Revelstoke is the largest part and mostly steep sport climbing, with crags like Begbie Bluffs and Blanket Canyon and some multipitch trad nearby. The Bugaboos are the alpine heart of the region, with long trad and alpine routes on spires. Rogers Pass, in the Selkirks inside Glacier National Park, offers alpine ridge routes, and some of its peaks have good quartzite. Roped climbing here runs from about 5.4 to 5.13, with the largest group at 5.10, and there is some water ice at WI3 to WI5. Sport leads in numbers, followed by trad and alpine; bouldering is minor.

ca_stoney_point.blurb: Stoney Point is a small urban crag in Chatsworth, in the San Fernando Valley north of Los Angeles, made of short cliffs and many boulders. The sandstone is fine-grained and compact, kind to the skin, but soft: holds break, so problems change over time, and it needs days to dry after rain. Bouldering dominates, with top-rope walls and canyons beside it and a few trad lines; it is not a sport crag. Boulder problems range from the easiest grades to about V10 with plenty of easy and moderate ones, and roped climbs run from about 5.4 to 5.12. Turlock, Boulder 1, the Canyon Boulders and the Summit Boulders are the largest areas. It climbs year-round, but summer gets very hot.

on_niagara_glen.blurb: Niagara Glen is the largest developed bouldering area in southern Ontario, in the gorge near Niagara Falls but quiet and wooded, with boulders clustered between the cliff and the river. It is all bouldering, with a broad spread from V0 to about V11 and plenty of moderates. The rock polishes easily, so many classics feel nearly frictionless, and the styles range from pocketed overhangs to thin crimps and slopers. Landings and rock quality vary a lot from one boulder to the next. Ten sectors share the problems, led by Old Country, Romper Room, Land of Oz and Wonderland, with Central and Bizzaro World also well stocked.

al_little_river_canyon.blurb: Little River Canyon, near Fort Payne in northeast Alabama, is a sport climbing area on high-quality sandstone, with walls stacked along the canyon among forested uplands, waterfalls and canyon rims. The climbing is steep and often powerful, with some thin technical and vertical sections. It is hard by design: very few routes sit below 5.11, most fall in the 5.11 to 5.13 range, and a few reach 5.14, so it suits experienced climbers. Tourist Wall, Lizard Wall, Toomsuba and Brandnewbia are among the biggest crags. The season is practically year-round, and Lizard Wall tends to stay dry when other walls are soaked, which makes it a fallback after rain.
